videos.title: Beyond the vault: Why AI agents force us to rethink Privileged Access Management (PAM)
videos.description:
Rohit Agnihotri has spent nearly two decades helping organizations rethink identity, building and leading IAM programs and advising executives on strategy. He's also the founder and host of the widely listened to Identity Navigator podcast. In this episode of Identity Decoded, he joins Roy Akerman and Rob Ainscough to make the case that traditional, vaulting-first privileged access management is dead, and to unpack what's replacing it. Rohit walks through why the old "vault everything" model breaks down under the sheer volume of machine identities, why standing privileges are one of the biggest attack vectors in the enterprise, and why organizations are shifting from vaulting to just-in-time access and, ultimately, zero standing privileges. The conversation turns to agentic AI, where Rohit introduces his own "Identity Uncertainty Principle": as an agent's autonomy increases, certainty about whether it's still the same agent you started with decreases. Together, they explore what that means for privilege, behavioral analytics, and why every autonomous agent needs a kill switch.

Key Topics
1. Why the old, vaulting-first model of PAM is dead
2. Moving from vaulting to just-in-time access to zero standing privileges
3. The Identity Uncertainty Principle: why more autonomous agents are less certain
4. Why every agentic AI identity needs a kill switch, not just a session timeout

🎧 Episode Highlights

[01:37]: Rohit's identity journey, from backend developer to IAM leader
[03:27]: Why the traditional, vaulting-first PAM model is dead
[07:57]: The rise of the authorization plane, and why brokered access is the future
[14:21]: Introducing the Identity Uncertainty Principle for agentic AI
[21:37]: Why agentic AI security can't be session-based, and the case for a kill switch
[26:33]: Rapid-fire round: identity myths, hard truths, and the most over hyped term in the industry

🔑 Key Takeaways:
● Vaulting credentials doesn't scale to machine identities. With machine identities projected to outnumber human ones by as much as 82ish to1 or more, vaulting every credential becomes too expensive to license, too static for identities that spin up and disappear, and too painful to review. Organizations are moving from vaulting to just-in-time access, and ultimately toward zero standing privileges.

● "What identities are privileged?" is becoming the wrong question to ask. Every organization defines privilege differently, and that inconsistency breaks down further with AI agents. Rather than asking how privileged an identity is, security teams are better served asking how much freedom it has to act, and what outcomes and risks that freedom creates.

● The more autonomous agents are, by definition, the less predictable they are, too. Rohit's Identity Uncertainty Principle holds that as an agent's autonomy increases, certainty about whether it's still behaving as originally intended decreases. Because agents can chain tools and pathways in ways no one anticipated, and carry none of the guilt, shame, or job-related restraint that shapes human behavior, security teams need dynamic risk scoring, behavioral analytics built for agents rather than humans, and a kill switch that can act in real time, not just at the end of a session.

👤 Guest Spotlight:

Rohit Agnihotri

Rohit Agnihotri has spent nearly two decades turning identity and access management from a technical function into a strategic business lever. His path into identity began early in his career writing back-end code, before a move to a startup introduced him to single sign-on and identity federation — and he's been leaning into the discipline ever since. He has led IAM from every angle, as a developer, architect, consultant, and executive, building and leading global teams at organizations including Northwestern Mutual, KPMG, and Cyberinc across IGA, PAM, cloud identity, and Zero Trust transformation. Today, CISOs and business leaders trust him to drive enterprise-wide IAM strategy, align identity with cloud modernization and M&A, and build high-performance teams and future-proof operating models. He's also known across the industry for challenging conventional thinking on privileged access management and identity for agentic AI, including his own "Identity Uncertainty Principle," and is the founder and host of the widely listened to Identity Navigator podcast.

videos.title: Anthropic's War on Open Source AI
videos.description:
The story used to be "too dangerous to release." Now Anthropic says the danger is you owning open source AI at all.

Full episode: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZhephRRRKfg

This clip is from They Might Be Self-Aware episode 197. Hunter Powers and Daniel Bishop track the AI industry's story flip on open source AI: for years the line was that frontier models were too strong to release into the wild, and in the last few months it became a push to stop anyone from running open weights models on their own computer. Daniel maps who is pounding the war drums (the CEOs of Anthropic and Palantir, with echoes from OpenAI) and why "it has to be through a trusted partner" is where the whole trick is hiding. The other side gets its best shot: models without safeguards raise real cybersecurity and national security questions, and Daniel explains why that argument is not a nothing burger even if the slippery slope might be. Also in the clip: the McDonald's CEO analogy (it is the end of civilization if people can make hamburgers at home), why the campaign against Chinese AI models made Hunter more curious about them, a possible future of AI medical tourism where the newest model weights come home from China on a USB drive, and the online poker precedent, when professional players just flew to Canada for the day because the game stayed legal there. If the top model costs $200 an hour and the flight costs $1,500, the math does itself. What happens when owning your own AI model becomes something you travel for?

They Might Be Self-Aware is the AI podcast from The Blur, reported from inside the dissolving line between human and machine, not from a safe distance.

videos.title: 40. Duty-Distinct Chain-of-Thought (DDCoT) Explained | Advanced Multimodal AI Prompt Engineering
videos.description:
How can AI accurately reason about images, documents, videos, and text without hallucinating? In this video, you'll learn **Duty-Distinct Chain-of-Thought (DDCoT)**, an advanced prompt engineering framework that improves multimodal AI reasoning by separating logical reasoning from visual understanding.

Unlike traditional Chain of Thought (CoT), DDCoT assigns different responsibilities to language models and vision models. It also introduces **negative-space prompting**, allowing the AI to explicitly identify missing or uncertain information before generating an answer. This results in more reliable, explainable, and trustworthy AI systems.

If you're building Vision AI, AI Agents, Multimodal LLM applications, or preparing for Generative AI interviews, DDCoT is a cutting-edge reasoning technique you should understand.

📚 In this video you'll learn:
✔ What is Duty-Distinct Chain-of-Thought (DDCoT)?
✔ Why Multimodal AI Hallucinates
✔ Separating Vision and Reasoning Tasks
✔ Negative-Space Prompting Explained
✔ Visual Understanding vs Logical Reasoning
✔ Sub-Question Decomposition
✔ Certain vs Uncertain Information
✔ Multimodal Prompt Engineering
✔ DDCoT vs Chain of Thought (CoT)
✔ Improving AI Explainability
✔ Reducing AI Hallucinations
✔ Advantages & Limitations

🔄 DDCoT Workflow:

1️⃣ Receive a Multimodal Input (Image + Text)

2️⃣ Break the Problem into Smaller Sub-Questions

3️⃣ Assign Vision Tasks to Vision Models

4️⃣ Assign Logical Reasoning to the LLM

5️⃣ Mark Missing Information Using Negative-Space Prompting

6️⃣ Combine Verified Results

7️⃣ Generate a Transparent and Accurate Final Answer

Key Concepts Covered:
• Duty-Distinct Chain-of-Thought (DDCoT)
• Prompt Engineering
• Multimodal AI
• Vision Language Models (VLMs)
• Negative-Space Prompting
• AI Hallucinations
• Explainable AI (XAI)
• Sub-Question Decomposition
• Logical Reasoning
• Visual Reasoning
• AI Agents
• Multimodal Prompting

Benefits:
✅ Better Multimodal Reasoning
✅ Fewer AI Hallucinations
✅ Improved Explainability
✅ Higher Accuracy
✅ Better Image Understanding
✅ Stronger AI Decision Making
✅ More Reliable AI Systems

Limitations:
❌ Higher Computational Cost
❌ More Complex AI Architecture
❌ Requires Multiple AI Models
❌ Increased Inference Time

Real-world Applications:
🖼️ Vision AI Systems
📄 Document Intelligence
🤖 AI Agents
🚗 Autonomous Vehicles
🏥 Medical Image Analysis
🛒 Retail Image Recognition
🔍 Visual Question Answering (VQA)

📚 Anyone Learning Prompt Engineering

By the end of this video, you'll understand how Duty-Distinct Chain-of-Thought separates vision and reasoning responsibilities, leverages negative-space prompting to identify uncertainty, and enables multimodal AI systems to generate more accurate, transparent, and trustworthy responses.

videos.title: ABot-N1: Dual-System Vision-Language Navigation
videos.description: In this AI Research Roundup episode, Alex discusses the paper: 'ABot-N1: Toward a General Visual Language Navigation Foundation Model' ABot-N1 is a new dual-system Visual Language Navigation (VLN) foundation model designed to solve the limitations of monolithic end-to-end architectures. It decouples cognition from control by using a slow-fast architecture that splits tasks between a deliberative reasoner and an action expert. The slow system uses a 4B-parameter multimodal model to perform chain-of-thought reasoning and project 2D pixel goals onto the robot's view. Meanwhile, the fast system runs at a high frequency to track these goals and output continuous waypoints for safe navigation. This approach effectively addresses coordinate drift, long-tail semantics, and gradient interference across heterogeneous tasks. Paper URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10383 #AI #MachineLearning #DeepLearning #Robotics #VisualLanguageNavigation #VLN #FoundationModels

videos.description:

Sign up for our free trending papers email digest: https://www.emergentmind.com/subscribe

This presentation explores GenCeption, a paradigm-shifting approach that repurposes large-scale video generation models as universal vision learners. Rather than building specialized architectures for each perception task, the researchers demonstrate that a single diffusion model pretrained to generate videos can perform depth estimation, segmentation, pose detection, and more through unified text conditioning. The work achieves state-of-the-art results across diverse tasks with dramatically less training data, marking a decisive step toward general-purpose vision foundation models analogous to large language models.

videos.title: The AI workflow that kills your plan before you start (no agents)
videos.description:
It's six months from now. The project you are excited about today has failed. Not struggling. Failed.

Now answer: why?

That is a different question from "what could go wrong". One asks you to speculate. The other tells you the ending and makes you explain it. And the difference is not wording. A 1989 study found that imagining a failure as something that has already happened makes people produce roughly 30% more reasons for it, and more concrete ones.

I built that question into a workflow and ran it on a real B2B analytics launch plan. The interesting result was not the verdict. It was where five reviewers who could not see each other's work ended up agreeing.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

CHAPTERS

0:00 A thought experiment
0:20 The 1989 finding
0:49 What actually replicates, and the fair criticism
1:29 The workflow, top to bottom
2:24 The plan I gave it
2:44 Five lenses, sealed off from each other
3:25 The web search they are not allowed to see
3:52 Thirteen risks, and the column that matters
4:32 Criticality is arithmetic, not opinion
5:06 The verdict, and what it is allowed to act on
5:46 Run it on your own plan

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

WHAT THE WORKFLOW DOES

It wraps your plan, unchanged, in a fixed frame: it is now the horizon, this plan was executed, it failed completely, the failure is certain, explain why.

It builds four to six failure lenses from your plan. Each lens writes its account alone and in parallel, and cannot see the others. Alongside them it runs a web search on how plans like yours really fail, and deliberately keeps that away from the writers, so all five cannot anchor on the same articles. The evidence arrives afterwards, at consolidation, as a referee.

Then it merges the accounts, removes duplicates, and records which lenses independently produced each cause. Criticality is computed in code as likelihood times impact. Every risk gets a proportionate response and a kill criterion. Then a viability verdict, and only if the plan fails does it write the revision advice.

In the run you are watching: 5 lenses, 13 consolidated risks, nine grounded and four plausible. The top risk was raised independently by three separate lenses: execution, engineering and budget. Verdict: not viable.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

THE RESEARCH

Mitchell, D. J., Russo, J. E., & Pennington, N. (1989). Back to the future: Temporal perspective in the explanation of events. Journal of Behavioral Decision Making, 2(1), 25-38. When an outcome is presented as certain and already in the past, people generate substantially more reasons for it, and more concrete ones. It is the certainty that does the work, not merely thinking about the future.
https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/bdm.3960020103

Klein, G. (2007). Performing a Project Premortem. Harvard Business Review. Assume the failure happened, generate the reasons independently, then consolidate.
https://www.researchgate.net/publication/3229642_Performing_a_Project_Premortem

Veinott, B., Klein, G., & Wiggins, S. (2010). Evaluating the Effectiveness of the PreMortem Technique on Plan Confidence. ISCRAM. 178 participants, several control conditions. The premortem reduced overconfidence more reliably than every comparison. The proven benefit is calibration, not alarm.
https://idl.iscram.org/files/veinott/2010/1049_Veinott_etal2010.pdf

On independent written generation before group discussion, which is why the lenses are sealed:
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6493673/

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

THE FAIR CRITICISM, AND THE ANSWER TO IT

The 1989 paper contains its own caveat: certainty framing produces more reasons, not necessarily better ones. Run a premortem carelessly and you bury a good plan under imagined threats, then damage it defending against things that were never likely.

So every risk is screened against the outside evidence and labelled grounded, plausible or speculative. Nothing is deleted, but nothing gets to sound more certain than it has earned. A speculative risk is only ever allowed to become something you watch: it can be a tripwire, it cannot change your plan. And a speculative risk, on its own, cannot vote your plan down. Only grounded risks can.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

RUN IT YOURSELF

The plan and the horizon are just fields. Paste in your own launch, migration, hire, funding round or product bet.

Sign up free at https://stewai.com and find it in the marketplace under "M002 Project Premortem".

StewAI is early, and the marketplace is being built with the people using it.

Docs: https://docs.stewai.com
Blog: https://stewai.com/blog

videos.title: 54GB to 3.9GB?! 1-Bit Models Just Changed Local AI | Kimi K3 Could Drop Tomorrow
videos.description:
Kimi K3 is rumored to be dropping soon, but the bigger story may be what’s happening with 1-bit AI models.

Bonsai 27B takes a model that would normally require roughly 54GB at FP16 and compresses it to around 3.9GB while retaining approximately 90% of its original intelligence. A capable 27B model can now run locally on everyday consumer devices—and even high-end phones.

That changes how we should think about the future of local AI.

Models are continuing to grow from hundreds of billions toward potentially trillions of parameters. Running those enormous models locally at 4-bit, 8-bit, or 16-bit precision will become increasingly difficult. However, if 1-bit and 2-bit compression keeps improving, we may still be able to run highly capable versions of those models on personal hardware.

A massive model running at 1-bit could potentially outperform a smaller model running at 4-bit or even 8-bit precision. That could make extreme low-bit compression the new standard for local AI.

In this video, I discuss the rumored Kimi K3 and K3 Agent Swarm release, Bonsai 27B, 1-bit and 1.58-bit models, model compression, local inference, and what this could mean for future frontier-class models.

My current workflow is simple:

I build with cloud models and maintain with local models.

Frontier models can handle the most demanding creation and development work. Once everything is built, local models can operate, maintain, automate, and execute those workflows without creating a permanent cloud bill.

The optimization happening in the open-source community is moving incredibly fast. Models are getting smaller, faster, and easier to run without sacrificing as much intelligence as we once expected.

The future of local AI may not be about buying unlimited hardware. It may be about fitting far more intelligence into every available bit.

Let me know what you think. Are 1-bit models the future, and would you run a compressed frontier-class model locally?

videos.title: Tool Calling Explained: How AI Agents Actually Work
videos.description:
What is tool calling — also called function calling — and how does it let an
AI agent actually DO things? In 18 minutes we open the door on the one
mechanism behind every agent: the tool list and JSON Schema the model sees,
the call it writes (and how it fills in the arguments), who really executes
it (the harness — never the model), and how the result comes back as text.
Then we go under the hood: why a tool call is just a message in one
transcript, why the JSON never breaks (and why valid ≠ correct), tool choice
(auto / required / none), chaining, parallel tool calls, and the small step
that turns tool calling into a full AI agent.

One live example runs through the whole video: an agent fixing a login bug
in twelve seconds — by the end, you can read every line of that trace.

CHAPTERS
0:00 Function calling: the building block of every AI agent
1:32 What we'll cover
2:09 Chapter 1: The Gap
2:24 Text in, text out — a model's three hard limits
3:34 The trick: actions as text (the work order)
4:51 Chapter 2: The Round Trip — the tool-call lifecycle
5:13 The tool list: names, descriptions, JSON Schema
6:22 The call: how the model picks tools and fills arguments
7:32 Who executes a tool call (the harness, not the model)
8:34 The answer: one full round trip
9:24 Chapter 3: Under the Hood
9:45 It's all one conversation: messages, statelessness, context
10:55 Why the JSON never breaks — and why valid ≠ correct
12:04 Tool choice: auto, required, none
13:03 Chapter 4: Many Calls — chaining & parallelism
13:25 Chaining: each result feeds the next call
14:36 Parallel tool calls (pause and decide)
15:49 From tool calling to AI agents
16:38 Recap: read the whole trace
17:38 Outro

New here? We draw one software concept per episode, clearly.

Gao Jiyang is the Founder and CEO of Galaxea. He received his bachelor’s degree in Electronic Engineering from Tsinghua University and later earned a Ph.D. in Computer Vision from the University of Southern California (USC). Prior to founding Galaxea, he worked at Waymo (Google’s self-driving car company) and the autonomous driving firm Momenta, where he was deeply involved in the development and deployment of core autonomous driving technologies. In 2023, he founded Galaxea, focusing on foundational models for embodied intelligence and robotic systems. The company’s valuation has already reached the tens of billions.
